statement: Session agenda (week 2, day 1): relational databases, understood briefly since everyone has used them, with most of the time spent on locking, especially pessimistic locking.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So the agenda for today is relational databases.

statement: No matter how many NoSQL databases come out (MongoDB, Cassandra, DynamoDB), relational databases hold a really special place: they are the heart and soul of business and form the raw foundation of how data should be structured and what guarantees a database can provide.
detail: The teacher calls them the world's strictest databases.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: No matter how many NoSQL comes in, no matter how many MongoDBs, Cassandras, and DynamoDBs come out, relational databases hold a really special place.

statement: Pessimistic locking is one of the most neglected topics in databases; people are scared of it, yet it is one of the best database features and helps you understand many things.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: This is one of the most neglected topics, if I may put it, of all time

statement: Lecture plan: first theory of locking, then a live demo in which an airline check-in system is actually coded to show how locking impacts everything; then a five-to-six-minute break; then a long discussion on building a key-value store on top of a relational database.
detail: The whole session focuses on relational databases.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: we'll build an airline check-in system, right?

statement: A key-value store on a relational DB means offering a key-value-store-like interface while the backend is a relational database; building it solidifies understanding of both relational DBs and key-value stores.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: we want to have a key-value store like thing, but on the backend, we will be having a relational DB.

statement: A relational database stores and represents data in rows and columns; its key highlight is relations, which is why it is called relational.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It's stored and represented in rows and columns. And the key highlight of that is relations, because of which they are called relational databases.

statement: Relational databases made much of today's technology possible: they were so good and reliable that everyone used them and built different applications on them, and they are now the backbone of the entire internet.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: And they are right now the backbone of our entire internet.

statement: Whenever a new revolutionary, foundational technology comes up, its first set of applications is always in finance (money, accounting); nothing magical about it, because society runs on money.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: a new revolutionary technology comes up, it would always find its first set of application in the domain of finance.

statement: When computers first came up, among the first applications ported to them were spreadsheets, basically called ledgers; the teacher's father used a black-and-white-screen machine with a tool called TW (typewriter) and a ledger tool to punch in numbers and do accounting.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Spreadsheet was one of the first, basically it was called ledger.

statement: Blockchain, introduced around 2012, found its first applications around money.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: the first set of applications that it found was around money.

statement: Relational databases were also meant for financial applications (accounting), which is why their structure is rows and columns.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Relational databases are also meant to do that exact same thing. That's why you see rows and columns as the structure.

statement: Because relational databases were conceptualized to make financial applications possible and dealt with money, they had to provide very strong guarantees, which is why ACID became a core part of them.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: they had to provide very strong guarantees because it was dealing with money, which is why ACID became the core part of this database.

statement: Financial use meant you cannot lose data or a transaction, whatever you write must be correct and never corrupted, and multiple people must be able to update it; so transactions became the core component of relational databases.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You cannot lose a transaction. Whatever you write has to be correct.

statement: Pre-reads: four articles by the teacher on A, C, I and D (ACID) and a video on how indexes make database reads faster; a members-only YouTube video on why databases use B+ trees comes out tomorrow.
detail: The teacher promises to make the class fall in love with relational databases by the end of the day.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: in the pre-reads, I shared four articles written by me on A, C, I and D.

statement: Anyone can create database tables and columns; the crux is how and why you do locking.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: the crux part is how to do locking, why do you do locking, why do we need locking.

statement: All relational databases (MySQL, Postgres, Oracle) give constructs that ensure your data does not get corrupted; one way is database locking, which is the pessimistic implementation.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: One of the ways to do it is with database locking, which is pessimistic implementation.

statement: When a transaction updates a critical row, no other transaction should do anything with that row at the same time, because an operation like count++ is not atomic.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: count plus plus is not atomic operation.

statement: Classic pessimistic locking: wrap the critical section with a lock; every transaction waits to acquire the lock, does the critical action, then releases it; only after release is another transaction allowed to do the operation.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: all the transaction would have to wait to acquire the lock, then do the critical action and then release the lock.

statement: There are two pessimistic locking strategies: shared lock and exclusive lock.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: There are two types of locking strategies. Pessimistic locking strategies. First is shared lock. Second is exclusive lock.

statement: Letting only one transaction do something at a time does slow down throughput.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So then wouldn't it slow down the throughput and all? Yes, it does affect, right?

statement: Two people clap on a Medium article at the same time: if both transactions read the same old count and both update it, the final value is count + 1 instead of the expected count + 2.
case_study: Medium clap count: two simultaneous claps lose one increment without locking.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: If both read the same old value, both updated, then the final value would be count plus one and not count plus two.

statement: Take locks before updating a row where correctness (sanity) of data matters more than throughput; where correctness is not important, it is okay to skip locking.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: this is where you need to have the correctness of data is more important than throughput. That's where locking comes in.

statement: Taking the necessary locks lets the database move from one consistent (correct) state to another correct state.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: allow you to have your database moving from one consistent state to, or one correct state to another correct state.

statement: Deadlock is a side effect of pessimistic locking that comes out of the box, unannounced.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: a very interesting side effect of it that comes out of the box, that comes unannounced, is deadlock.

statement: Transactional deadlock: T1 wants a lock on row 1, which is held by T2; T2 wants a lock on row 2, which is held by T1; nobody moves forward. It is the same deadlock studied in operating systems.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Transaction T2 wants a lock on row 2, but row 2 is acquired by T1.

statement: Whenever you add pessimistic locking you are risking a deadlock, always, because you never know how threads are scheduled or who is waiting on what.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: whenever you add pessimistic locking, you are risking a deadlock. Always. Always.

statement: Whenever you write code or a SQL query that takes locks, in any language, check whether it can lead to a deadlock: arrange your statements and the order of lock acquisition and release, and if a deadlock is possible, protect against it.
detail: The teacher says the class will spend time on deadlock protection too.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Try to arrange your statements, try to arrange your lock, acquisition and release such that it can really enter a deadlock or not.

statement: Transactional deadlocks are killers: they stall your database.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: But transactional deadlocks are killers. They stall your database.

statement: Most popular databases (MySQL, Postgres, Oracle) do not let the database enter a deadlock state.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: is they do not let the database enter a deadlock state

statement: Every time the database locks a row for a transaction, it runs a deadlock detection algorithm to check whether granting that lock would put the database into a deadlock.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: every time you're locking a particular row, your database would run a deadlock detection algorithm.

statement: Deadlock detection is simple: a cyclic path (in the wait-for relationships) means a deadlock.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Deadlock detection is simple: whenever you have a cyclic path in it, it's a deadlock.

statement: If granting a lock would create a deadlock (e.g. T1 asking for row 2 in the T1/T2 example), the database engine kills the transaction that fired that query; this way a cyclic dependency edge is never allowed to form.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: that transaction will be killed by the database engine.

statement: You can easily reproduce this locally: start two transactions, have two rows, acquire locks crosswise; when the final lock-acquiring query fires, the transaction that fired it is killed.
detail: The teacher says the demo will show how to mimic it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Just start two transactions, have two rows, acquiring lock, acquiring lock.

statement: If a database enters a deadlock state everything stalls and nothing moves forward; the only way to recover is rebooting the database, which means downtime, so databases never let it happen.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: The only way to recover from that is to reboot the database, which means downtime.

statement: Core computer science (deadlock detection and prevention) is not going anywhere no matter how many React-like frameworks come out; it applies not just to databases but to operating system threads and distributed transactions.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Core computer science is not going anywhere. No matter how many React comes out, core computer science is core computer science.

statement: Most databases offer two lock types: shared locks, also called read locks, and exclusive locks, also called write locks.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: First are shared locks, but they are also called as read locks. And there are exclusive locks, also called as write locks.

statement: To take a shared lock in SQL, write a normal SELECT and end it with FOR SHARE; the transaction gets a shared lock on every row the query matched.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You write your normal select statement and just end it with for share.

statement: With six rows, transaction T1 runs a SELECT ... FOR SHARE matching rows 1, 2 and 6 and, once it executes, holds shared locks on rows 1, 2 and 6.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: transaction T1 would have shared locks on row 1, 2 and 6.

statement: Another transaction T2 fires SELECT ... WHERE user_id IN (3, 4, 6) FOR SHARE and also gets shared locks, on rows 3, 4 and 6, even though row 6 is shared-locked by T1.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: select where user ID in 3, 4, 6 for share.

statement: A shared (read) lock lets the holding transaction read the row and also lets other transactions read it, but other transactions are not allowed to modify it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: when one transaction is having a read lock on it, other transactions are allowed to read them.

statement: If T1 holds the shared lock on rows 1, 2, 6 and T2 tries to update row 6, T2 has to wait until T1 commits or aborts: T1 may read and modify the row, T2 may only read it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So if it tries to modify, it would have to wait until transaction 1 is either complete, or it is either committed or aborted.

statement: Shared locks give very high read throughput for read-heavy use cases: other transactions can still read the locked rows, while modification is prevented.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So when you are using shared lock, you get very high read throughput.

statement: If a transaction holding a shared lock on rows itself modifies them, the read lock is elevated to an exclusive lock implicitly (you do nothing) and only then the modification happens.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: read lock gets elevated to an exclusive lock and then only modification happens.

statement: Whenever a transaction wants to update a row, it has to take an exclusive lock on it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: whenever a transaction wants to update a particular row, it has to take an exclusive lock.

statement: An exclusive lock is really strict: other transactions are not even allowed to read the locked rows, let alone modify them.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: exclusive lock is the, is really strict, where it does not even allow other transactions to even read the locked rows.

statement: To take an exclusive lock, end the SELECT with FOR UPDATE: the rows selected by the query are exclusively locked by the transaction.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: When you end your SQL query with for update

statement: If T1 holds exclusive locks on rows 1, 2, 6 (FOR UPDATE), a T2 query wanting rows 3, 4, 6 does not complete: it waits until T1 commits or aborts because of row 6; without row 6 in its set, T2's statement would have completed with rows 3 and 4.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: this SQL query would not complete. Why? Because it is wanting to read a row 6 which is locked by transaction 1 at this moment.

statement: Exclusive locks severely impact throughput, but where you need exclusivity you have to use them.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It severely impacts the throughput, but where you need exclusivity, you have to do it.

statement: SQL databases provide shared and exclusive locks out of the box to ensure correctness of your system under concurrent transactions.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: they give you shared locks and exclusive locks out of the box

statement: SKIP LOCKED (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED): if any of the rows the query wants are locked by another transaction, skip them and proceed on a best-effort basis with the unlocked rows instead of waiting.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: if any of those rows are locked by some other transaction, skip them.

statement: With T1 holding rows 1, 2, 6, a T2 query for rows 3, 4, 6 with SKIP LOCKED moves forward immediately and gets only rows 3 and 4.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: this transaction would have moved forward and I would have gotten only rows three and four.

statement: Use SKIP LOCKED when your use case is fine working with whatever rows are not locked; when you need all the rows, you have to wait, there is no other option.
detail: The teacher says such use cases will be seen shortly (the demo).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: But there are some cases where you have to wait, where you need all these three rows there. So then you have to wait.

statement: NOWAIT is the other extreme of SKIP LOCKED: if any of the rows the query wants is locked by another transaction, the transaction kills itself instead of waiting.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Another extreme of skip lock is no wait.

statement: With NOWAIT the transaction is in an existential crisis: someone else has picked that row and will process it, so it has no reason to exist and kills itself.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Like, that transaction is going into existential crisis.

statement: After a NOWAIT failure the transaction can retry or not, depending on your business.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you kill yourself and then maybe retry and all, depending on your business.

statement: NOWAIT exists so you do not wait unnecessarily: otherwise T2 waits for the lock up to the SQL query timeout (say 10 seconds), choking database performance for that thread and making the client wait, when the use case does not care if the row is locked.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: let's say your SQL query timeout is, let's say, 10 seconds. So it would wait for 10 seconds unnecessarily.

statement: Learn by implementing the core of a system, the part you are interested in, rather than the whole system: the demo implements only the database part of an airline check-in system to understand database locks; you do not need to write CRUD for everything, just small prototypes.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Understand the core of the system and implement it. That's how you learn.

statement: Students implemented all four of short polling, long polling, SSE and WebSockets (previous week's material); the teacher encourages implementing because that is where you learn most.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I was so happy to see folks trying out all the four, like short polling, long polling,

statement: About 85% of what the teacher talks about he has built himself, so he knows where those systems falter in production; anyone can draw high-level boxes, but knowing the implementation details is what makes you a better architect.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: All of these things that I'm talking about, 85% of them is something that I've built myself.

statement: Airline check-in prototype data model: multiple airlines (Air India, Indigo, Go Air), each airline has multiple flights, each flight has 120 seats (oversimplified), each flight has multiple trips, and a user books a seat in one trip of a flight.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Each flight has 120 seats, I'm just oversimplifying it, each flight has 120 seats.

statement: The check-in problem: handle multiple people trying to pick the same seat, so that all 120 seats get filled in the best way possible; the demo goes step by step to show where locking comes in.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: we have to handle multiple people trying to pick the same seat.

statement: Schema: airlines table (unique airlines); flights (flight id, airline id, flight name, e.g. Air India 101); trips (trip id, flight, fly and land times); users; and seats (for a trip, which user occupies which seat). For a new trip, every seat's user is initially null and filling it is the system's job.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: a seats table, where you are saying that, hey, on this trip, this seat is occupied by this user.

statement: High-level architecture: a check-in service, a relational database (MySQL, a no-brainer since the topic is relational DBs) and an admin service.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you have your check-in service, you have a database. Let's say I pick MySQL to do this

statement: The admin service creates, for every trip of every flight, one seat row per seat with user ID set to null when the flight is opened for booking; it also adds new flights and trips and keeps things updated.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you would have one entry for each seat with user ID set to null

statement: Demo data: a users table with 120 random names (user 1 'Maurya Harmon', ...), a trips table (trip 1 'Air India 1') and a seats table where, e.g., seat 1A of the trip is booked by user 4.
detail: A student asked whether the names came from the Faker library; the teacher only replied that he has 120 names.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I have 120 names. Then I have trips.

statement: The demo is not a reservation system: people have already booked and paid for the flight; they only pick a seat.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: what we are not doing is we are not reservation system. People have already booked the flight. Now they are here to pick a seat.

statement: Scenario: all 120 passengers of a flight reach the airport at the exact same moment and go to 120 kiosks to pick their seats simultaneously.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Now imagine all 120 people of a particular flight all reach the airport at the exact same moment.

statement: The demo walks through approaches 0 to 5 in mini steps to understand pessimistic database locking in depth.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Approach 0 to approach 5. Take mini steps to understand database locking, pessimistic locking, in depth.

statement: The demo code is in Go, which the teacher loves for its simplicity, elegance and easy concurrency; any language that supports concurrency works, otherwise you would need multiple processes to mimic it, and doing it with threads is much easier.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I love Golang because of its simplicity, because of its elegance, because of easy concurrency.

statement: Approach 0 (sanity check): the program takes a user ID as argument, asks which seat to book and books it; e.g. user 1 books seat 3, which shows as seat 1C booked by that user.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So first approach is very simple, just to see if everything is working or not.

statement: The seat layout follows a typical plane: 1A, 1B, 1C, 1D, 1E, 1F, 2A ... 2F, and so on.
speaker: teacher

statement: Approach 0 book function: begin a transaction, SELECT the seat by ID, UPDATE seats SET user_id = ? WHERE id = ?, then commit.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Update seats set user ID equal to question mark where user ID is this and ID equal to this

statement: Approach 0 has zero checks: it does not check whether the seat is already booked, so another user can book the exact same seat; naive, but it lays the foundation.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Which means that tomorrow I can have another user coming in and can book the exact same seat, and my system would not prevent that

statement: Letting users book any seat ID leads to two people booking the same seat, both boarding passes being printed and chaos in the plane.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: both of their boarding passes getting printed and there's a chaos in the plane.

statement: Approach 1: instead of the user choosing, the system picks a seat at random from all the seats of the airplane (not just the available ones) and assigns it with the same unchecked UPDATE, relying only on the random function.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: airline.seats gives me all the seats of the airplane, not all the available seats, all the seats of the airplane.

statement: Approach 1 can still give two people the same seat: the random function can easily pick the same seat in two iterations.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It's very likely for this random function to pick the same seat in two different iterations.

statement: Approach 2 simulates concurrency: when main starts, a goroutine is spawned for each of the 120 users, all trying to pick a seat at the same time; book(user) picks a random seat, starts a transaction, updates and commits.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I'm simulating all 120 users coming into my system at the exact same time and trying to book a seat.

statement: A goroutine is like a thread running in its own space.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Goroutine is like a thread, like a thread which is running in its own space

statement: Asked what approach 2 will do, a student predicts some users will get the same seats and not all seats will be filled; whether seats come out unique depends on how the RAND function is implemented. The teacher replies 'Correct'.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: So some users will get the same seats, as you said

statement: Running approach 2: not all seats are filled, because the random function, called 120 times, did not pick 120 unique values; several passengers end up holding the same seat (two people would fight in the air both claiming 7C).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: we see that RANDUP function did not pick 120 unique values, it repick some of the values

statement: Approach 3: pick the first unoccupied seat with SELECT id, name, trip_id, user_id FROM seats WHERE trip_id = 1 AND user_id IS NULL ORDER BY id LIMIT 1, then update that seat and commit; again run for 120 users in parallel.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: order by id limit one. I'm picking the first seat that I can find which is not occupied by anyone

statement: A student argues approach 3 will not fill all seats: concurrent transactions accessing at the exact same time both see the seat's user as null, so the same seat is offered to several people unless some locking is in place. The teacher agrees: this is exactly why locking is needed.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: So both of them are accessing at the exact same time and, yeah, the database is giving the same value to both of them

statement: Locking is needed because transactions running at the exact same time may see the exact same value and operate on it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Because both the transactions running at that exact same time might see the exact same value and operate with that.

statement: Asked which seat gets booked, students say everyone tries to book the first seat because of LIMIT 1 / ORDER BY id LIMIT 1; the teacher refines: ORDER BY is the reason.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: Order by ID limit one.

statement: In approach 3, because of ORDER BY id, all concurrent transactions see seat ID 1 first (then 2, 3 in order) and everyone books that same seat.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Order by is the reason. Because of order by, everyone will get seat one, two, three in that order.

statement: Two students predict that in approach 3 only one seat will be booked.
detail: When run (00:46:08), the demo filled two to four seats, depending on the run; the teacher does not respond to the prediction directly.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: One seat.

statement: A student predicts that every concurrent read returns 1A so every write targets that row, and multiple seats get booked only if some transaction has already committed its update before another read happens.
detail: The teacher does not comment directly but runs the demo; his explanation at 00:47:48 (commit before the next read) matches.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: Case multiple seats will be booked only if update has happened and after which another read is happening

statement: Running approach 3: a few seats get filled in order (seats 1, 2, 3 one run, four seats another, two seats another); there is no guarantee how many seats get filled, and the logs show the same seat (e.g. 1C) assigned repeatedly.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: there is no guarantee that exactly n seats will be filled

statement: In approach 3, if all 120 transactions start while the first seat is still free, all of them book that one seat.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: In that case everyone would see only one seat, like everyone would be booking that one seat.

statement: Approach 3 fills more than one seat only because some goroutine committed before a later one read: the later read sees seat 1's user_id as not null and, via the WHERE user_id IS NULL condition, picks the next row; it is the condition, not the code or the transaction, that moves it on.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: it got the next row because of this condition, not because this is how we wrote the code.

statement: This is why commit matters: once a transaction commits, any transaction that reads after it sees the committed value.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: This is why commit is so important.

statement: Approach 3 shows why pessimistic locking is needed: the system was expected to fill all 120 seats, but it does not because everyone reads the same old row.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: because everyone is reading that same old row. This is exactly why pessimistic locking is needed.

statement: Approach 4: the exact approach 3 code with just two words added at the end of the SELECT: FOR UPDATE (pessimistic exclusive lock).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I just added two words at the end: for update.

statement: A student predicts approach 4 will deadlock: the second user waits for the first and its transaction may get cancelled. The teacher says no: waiting is not deadlock.
detail: Teacher's correction: deadlock happens when you wait on a row locked by someone who is in turn waiting for a row you hold; here transactions merely wait.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: Because the first user who is coming in, if he is acquiring a seat, okay. And the second one is also waiting for it.

statement: Waiting is not deadlock: deadlock happens when you wait on a row locked by someone else who is waiting for a row you hold.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Waiting is not equal to deadlock.

statement: A student predicts starvation in approach 4: all 120 seats will be filled because FOR UPDATE is a pessimistic lock, but not concurrently; waiting time grows for later transactions (e.g. the 10th waits longer).
detail: The teacher probes but gives no verdict here; the run at 01:00:02 does fill all 120 seats.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: I think there'll be starvation for some threads.

statement: A student reasons that in approach 4 a waiting transaction would read the locked first row and wait, so to move on there must be a verification step: once the lock is released, check that user_id is still null before writing, otherwise rows get rewritten. The teacher replies 'Not entirely true' and explains later.
detail: The teacher's later explanation (01:01:25): waiting transactions are signalled to re-evaluate the query when the lock holder commits.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: it needs to make sure that the user ID is still null and then you need to write.

statement: Q: Aren't ACID properties given by default, so why lock? A: ACID properties are at the transaction level; here there are concurrent transactions locking rows within a transaction, and how concurrent transactions are scheduled depends on the database's isolation level.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: ACID properties is at transaction level.

statement: Durability: when you commit, the data gets flushed.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So durability, when you commit, it gets flushed.

statement: Isolation means two running transactions are independent of each other; the isolation levels are read committed, read uncommitted, repeatable read and serializable, and transactions are scheduled according to the level.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Isolation, which means two transactions that running, they are independent of each other.

statement: Under the serializable isolation level the database does not execute another transaction while one is executing; transactions run literally one after another, which is pathetically slow, but you would not face the seat-booking problem at all.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: serializable isolation level says that when one transaction is executing, my database would not even execute other transaction

statement: The default isolation level is not serializable and you don't set it, for practical reasons: you need high throughput and parallel writes; a user updating row 100 should not wait for another user updating row 1.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: why should one updating row hundred should wait for row one to get updated?

statement: A student sums up: the ACID isolation behaviour is configurable, and in typical use cases it is not configured to serializable because of high throughput; the teacher confirms that with serializable you would not need all this locking.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: In typical use case, we don't configure it for high throughput.

statement: A student predicts approach 4 will not fill all 120 seats: SKIP LOCKED is not enabled by default, so every transaction tries to get the same first row and only one row gets filled.
detail: The run at 01:00:02 fills all 120 seats; the teacher gives no direct verdict on this prediction.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: I think so, because like skip lock is not available right now, so it won't move to second.

statement: Another student predicts approach 4 will fill somewhere between 1 and 120 seats, depending on goroutine scheduling, but not 120.
detail: The run at 01:00:02 fills all 120 seats.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: Not all 120, but somewhere between 1 to 120, I think.

statement: A student predicts all 120 seats will be filled in approach 4: FOR UPDATE takes an exclusive lock, so T2 and the others wait until row R1 is free; when T1 completes they see R1 is no longer null and move to R2. The teacher asks how the database would automatically move to the next row, then says the reasoning is almost 90% correct.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: So it will wait until R1 gets free.

statement: Think like the database engineer: the engine must handle both a range query (user_id IS NULL ORDER BY id LIMIT 1) and a pointed lookup (seat id = 67) in one uniform way; a pointed row lock would not move to the next row.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: There has to be a uniform way to handle both types of queries, right?

statement: A student predicts approach 4 will behave like approach 3: not all 120 filled; if something was committed a later thread picks another row, otherwise everybody waits on 1A, sees it filled and cancels.
detail: The run at 01:00:02 fills all 120 seats.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: No, I don't think that all 120 will get filled.

statement: If adding two words to a query makes no difference, something might be wrong.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: if we are adding two words to our query and it's still not making any difference, something might be wrong.

statement: Running approach 4 (FOR UPDATE): all 120 seats are filled, on every run.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: If I run it again, all 120 seats are filled up.

statement: In approach 4 seats are booked in order (1C, 1D, 1E, 1F, 2A, 2B, ...): each transaction takes an exclusive lock and, while it holds it, other transactions wait.
detail: The teacher calls the behind-the-scenes mechanism the most critical part that people skip.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So users are coming, they're taking an exclusive lock, and while that exclusive lock is taken, other transactions wait.

statement: Misconception: that all 120 concurrent transactions get the first row. The database does not return the row to a transaction until it gets the lock; the engine sees that the rows the query iterates over are locked by someone and makes the transaction wait.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Database is not returning the first row unless they get it.

statement: When the lock-holding transaction commits, the transactions waiting on it are signalled to re-execute and re-evaluate the query.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: when the first transaction commits, the other transactions waiting on it are signaled to re-execute and re-evaluate the query.
flags: unclear: "I'm not going to about state"

statement: Re-evaluation does not mean the client re-fires the query: the signalled transaction re-evaluates the same statement and tries to acquire the lock; since the first transaction committed, it now sees the second row.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It does not mean you have to re-fire the query.

statement: In approach 4 user 1 does not get seat 1, user 2 seat 2: whichever transaction gets scheduled first gets the next seat (seat 1A went to a different user than user 1).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It's that whichever transaction got scheduled first is getting it.

statement: Approach 4 behind the scenes: the first transaction acquires the lock and the rest wait; when it commits or aborts, the database engine signals the waiters to re-evaluate the query; one of the 119 acquires the lock on the second row; when it commits the rest are signalled for the third seat, fourth seat, and so on.
detail: The teacher first says 'operating system', then corrects himself to 'database engine'.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: When first transaction committed or aborted, other transactions are signaled by the operating system to move on, or rather database engine to move on.

statement: Approach 4 is painful for the database (repeated waiting and re-evaluation), but it guarantees correctness.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: it's so painful for the database to do this much of operation. But we are still guaranteeing the correctness of the system.

statement: Approach 5: the approach 4 query with SKIP LOCKED added at the end; since it is fine to move on when a row is locked, the database should not wait unnecessarily.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: the only two word change I'll do: at the end, I'll just add skip lock.

statement: A student predicts approach 5 will fill all seats while avoiding the busy waiting of approach 4, so total execution time will be less; the teacher agrees.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: The time of the execution of the transaction would be less.

statement: Approach 4 (FOR UPDATE) took 1.7 seconds; approach 5 (FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED) completed in 147 milliseconds, about one tenth of the time, and still filled all 120 seats.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: it just completed in 147 milliseconds. One 10th of the time

statement: With SKIP LOCKED the transaction still takes an exclusive lock, but when the engine sees a matching row is locked it quickly moves to the next row matching the WHERE clause and locks that one, so no transaction waits for the first to complete and rows are locked continuously by different transactions.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: None of the other transaction wait for the first one to complete

statement: Just adding SKIP LOCKED made the system 10x faster; this is why you need to know how your database actually does things, including locking.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You just made your system 10x faster just by adding skip lock, as simple as that.

statement: Those who say relational databases don't scale do not know their real power.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Relational databases don't scale. They don't know the real power of relational databases.

statement: Relational databases scale beautifully well; they cannot handle big data, but at scaling and handling high QPS they are champions; you only need to know performance tuning, and here that is just normal SQL query constructs, not nitty-gritty tuning.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Relational databases scale beautifully well. They cannot handle big data, I agree to that.

statement: Approach 0 to 5 evolved the system by adding just two or three words to the query: first make sure the system fails (approaches 0-3), then ensure correctness with an exclusive lock (FOR UPDATE), then add SKIP LOCKED for performance.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Then we ensure the correctness in the exclusive lock. Then we added skip lock to get the performance.
